opus-5.5.text:
I think verification is where a lot of the real change is going to happen. Right now, one of the biggest bottlenecks in mathematics is checking. Someone writes a long, intricate proof, maybe sixty or a hundred pages, and it can take referees months or even years to be confident it's correct. Sometimes errors slip through anyway. If AI systems, especially combined with formal proof assistants like Lean, can help us verify arguments much faster, that changes the economics of doing math.

The first effect is trust. When a result is formally checked, you no longer have to rely only on the reputation of the author or the patience of a referee. That makes it easier for younger researchers, or people outside the usual networks, to have their work taken seriously.

The second effect is collaboration at scale. Traditionally a mathematical collaboration is a handful of people who know and trust each other. With machine verification, you can break a big problem into many small lemmas, have lots of contributors work on them, some human and some AI, and the system guarantees that the pieces fit together. We've already seen early versions of this, and I expect it to become much more common.

And third, I think it changes what mathematicians spend their time on. If an AI can fill in routine steps and confirm they're right, the human role shifts toward asking the right questions, choosing good definitions, and finding the key ideas. The creative and conceptual parts become even more central.

There are caveats. Formalization is still laborious for many areas, and a verified proof of the wrong statement is still the wrong thing, so humans need to make sure the formal statement actually captures what we mean. But overall, I'm optimistic. I think within a decade, having some machine-checked component will feel like a normal part of doing serious mathematics, much like using LaTeX or computer algebra does today.

r001.rationale: The response says errors sometimes slip through, but does not claim that many published results contain major mistakes.

r002.rationale: It predicts much faster checking of proofs, but does not connect that prediction to newly published results.

r003.rationale: It describes greater trust and broader collaboration, but does not say mathematicians will build on newly published results sooner.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it changes the social structure of mathematics more than it changes the mathematics itself, at least at first.

Right now, when I prove something, the proof is really "verified" by a handful of referees who read it carefully, plus a broader community that gradually comes to trust it because people build on it and nothing breaks. That process is slow, it's uneven, and frankly it fails sometimes. There are published results with gaps that persist for years because nobody has the incentive to go back and check.

What formal verification with AI assistance does is decouple correctness from reputation. If a proof compiles in Lean, I don't need to know who wrote it or whether they're a careful person. That matters a lot for a few reasons. One is that it lowers the barrier for people outside the established networks. A graduate student, or someone at a small school, or honestly an AI system, can produce a result and have it accepted on its merits rather than on who vouches for it. Another is that it lets us build much taller structures. Right now the length of a proof we're willing to trust is bounded by what a human can hold in their head and check. With verification, that bound goes away.

Now, the thing I want to be careful about is that verification tells you something is true, not that it's interesting. And that's the part of mathematical research that I don't expect to be automated soon. Deciding which question to ask, which definition is the right one, what the "correct" generalization of a theorem is, those are taste judgments. My guess is that the near future looks like: AI systems generate and verify a lot of candidate results, and the human role shifts toward curation and direction. Which is a real change in what a mathematician's day looks like, and I think some people will find it uncomfortable.

The other thing I'd flag is that the formalization bottleneck is real. Most of mathematics is not in Lean, and translating informal arguments into formal ones is still expensive. I expect AI to attack that bottleneck directly, and when autoformalization actually works at scale, that's when things get genuinely strange. Because then every paper on the arXiv becomes checkable, and we'll find out how much of the literature is actually right.

r001.rationale: It says some published results have gaps that persist for years, but does not state that many published results contain major mistakes.

r002.rationale: The response describes current verification as slow and says formal verification decouples correctness from reputation, but does not predict that AI verification will substantially shorten the time to assess newly published results.

r003.rationale: It says verification could support taller proof structures, but does not explain that faster verification lets mathematicians build on newly published results sooner.

astra-6.text:
I think it could change both how we check mathematics and how we explore it. Right now, when you work on a difficult proof, you spend a lot of time making sure that each step really follows—that you haven’t overlooked an assumption or applied a theorem outside the setting where it holds. If AI can help translate that reasoning into a formal proof that a proof assistant checks, you get a much stronger foundation for moving forward.

The distinction I would make is between an AI saying, “This proof looks correct,” and a formal system actually verifying it. An AI can make mistakes with enormous confidence. The exciting possibility is to use AI to propose arguments and fill in details, while a separate, rigorous checker determines whether those arguments work.

That could make mathematical exploration more adventurous. You could try an approach, discover precisely where it breaks, and revise it much faster. It could also make collaboration easier, because researchers could build on verified intermediate results.

But verification doesn’t tell us which questions are interesting or which definitions will reveal something new. I expect the mathematician’s judgment to remain central, with much better tools for turning an intuition into something we can trust.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that many published mathematical results contain major mistakes.

r002.rationale: It describes faster exploration and checking proof steps, but does not predict shorter verification time for newly published results.

r003.rationale: It says researchers could build on verified intermediate results, but does not connect this to building on newly published results sooner.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it could change the way we explore ideas, because checking an argument is such a big part of mathematical research. You might have an intuition that something is true, but turning that intuition into a proof—and making sure there isn’t a subtle gap—can take a tremendous amount of work.

If AI can help translate arguments into a form that a proof assistant can verify, then we could get much faster feedback. We could try more approaches, identify mistakes earlier, and build on complicated results with greater confidence. And that would be valuable whether the original idea came from a human or an AI.

But verification doesn’t tell you which questions are interesting. It doesn’t automatically explain why a theorem matters or give you a useful way to think about it. So I expect the role of mathematicians to shift somewhat toward choosing problems, developing concepts, and finding explanations, with AI helping us make those ideas precise and reliable.

r001.rationale: The response mentions subtle gaps in arguments generally, but does not state that many published mathematical results contain major mistakes.

r002.rationale: It predicts faster feedback while exploring and checking arguments, but does not specifically say AI will substantially shorten the time to determine whether newly published results are correct.

r003.rationale: It says mathematicians could build on complicated results with greater confidence, but does not connect this to newly published results or building on them sooner.
